mcqs.q: X-rays were discovered in 1895 by:
mcqs.explain: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered x-rays in 1895 and is called the Father of Radiology.

mcqs.q: Ionizing radiation is defined as radiation that:
opts: Can produce ions by removing or adding an electron to an atom
mcqs.explain: Ionizing radiation produces ions by removing/adding an electron — converting a neutral atom into a charged ion.

mcqs.q: In Bohr's atomic model, the nucleus contains:
mcqs.explain: The nucleus holds protons (+1 charge) and neutrons (no charge); electrons (−) orbit around it.

mcqs.q: The maximum number of electron shells in an atom is ___, named:
opts: 7 — K, L, M, N, O, P, Q
mcqs.explain: There are up to 7 shells (K,L,M,N,O,P,Q) holding 2, 8, 18, 32… electrons respectively.

mcqs.q: An atom becomes an ION when it:
opts: Gains or loses electrons (becoming electrically unbalanced)
Loses a proton from the nucleus
mcqs.explain: Gaining an electron makes an atom negative; losing one makes it positive — either way it becomes an ion.

mcqs.q: For electromagnetic waves, as the wavelength becomes SHORTER:
opts: Frequency and energy increase, and penetration increases
mcqs.explain: Shorter wavelength → higher frequency → greater energy → the wave penetrates objects more easily.

mcqs.q: Which is a property of x-rays?
opts: No mass, no charge; travel at the speed of light in straight lines
Can be focused to a single point
mcqs.explain: X-rays have no mass or charge, travel at the speed of light in straight lines, are invisible, and cannot be focused to a point.

mcqs.q: The three main parts of the intra-oral x-ray machine are:
opts: Control panel, extension arm, and tube head
mcqs.explain: The x-ray machine consists of the control panel, the extension arm, and the tube head.

mcqs.q: The kVp setting primarily controls the:
opts: Energy / penetrating quality of the x-ray beam
mcqs.explain: kVp controls the energy (penetrating quality) of the beam; mA and time control quantity.

mcqs.q: The mA setting controls the:
opts: Heating of the filament and therefore the quantity of x-rays
mcqs.explain: mA determines filament heating: a hotter filament releases more electrons → more x-rays (quantity). Doubling mA doubles the number of x-rays.

mcqs.q: The Position-Indicating Device (PID) is an open-ended, lead-lined cylinder that:
opts: Aims and shapes the x-ray beam
mcqs.explain: The PID aims and shapes the x-ray beam; it comes in conical, rectangular and round (lead-lined) forms.

mcqs.q: The negative electrode of the x-ray tube (the cathode) consists of a:
opts: Tungsten filament in a molybdenum focusing cup
Tungsten target in a copper block
mcqs.explain: The cathode (−) is a tungsten filament (electron source) sitting in a molybdenum focusing cup that directs electrons onto the anode target.

mcqs.q: When the filament is heated and releases electrons, this process is called:
mcqs.explain: Heating the tungsten filament releases a cloud of electrons around it — thermionic emission; the hotter it is, the more electrons.

mcqs.q: The anode (positive electrode) target is made of tungsten because it:
opts: Converts the kinetic energy of electrons into x-ray photons (and tolerates heat)
mcqs.explain: The tungsten target converts the electrons' kinetic energy into x-ray photons; it sits in a copper block that dissipates the heat.

mcqs.q: The line-focus principle (angling the target ~17–20°) is used to:
opts: Produce a small focal spot for a sharper image
mcqs.explain: Angling the target gives a small effective focal spot — the smaller the focal spot, the sharper the image of the teeth.

mcqs.q: Which transformer is controlled by the kVp setting?
mcqs.explain: The step-up transformer (controlled by kVp) raises the voltage between cathode and anode; the step-down transformer (mA) lowers voltage to the filament.

mcqs.q: Most x-rays in the beam are produced by which mechanism?
mcqs.explain: Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) — a high-speed electron decelerated/deflected by the tungsten nucleus — produces the majority of x-rays.

mcqs.q: Characteristic radiation is produced when:
opts: An electron knocks out an inner-shell electron and an outer electron drops in
An electron is decelerated by the nucleus
A photon scatters off an outer electron
mcqs.explain: Characteristic radiation forms when a high-speed electron ejects an inner-shell electron; an outer-shell electron fills the vacancy, releasing a characteristic x-ray photon.

mcqs.q: Filtration of the x-ray beam (aluminium) is done to:
opts: Remove low-energy photons and reduce skin dose
mcqs.explain: Filtration removes low-energy (non-useful) photons, reducing patient skin dose. Total filtration is 1.5 mm Al up to 70 kVp, 2.5 mm above 70 kVp.

mcqs.q: Collimation of the x-ray beam controls the:
opts: Size and shape of the beam (reducing tissue exposure)
mcqs.explain: Collimation restricts the beam's size/shape; a rectangular collimator reduces exposure by ~60% compared with a round one.

mcqs.q: The inverse-square law states that x-ray beam intensity is:
opts: Inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source
mcqs.explain: Intensity ∝ 1/distance² — doubling the distance quarters the intensity.

mcqs.q: In photoelectric absorption, the incident photon:
opts: Ejects a bound (usually K-shell) electron and ceases to exist
Is scattered with the same frequency
Is deflected off an outer electron
mcqs.explain: In photoelectric absorption the photon collides with a bound (K-shell) electron, ejecting a recoil electron, and the photon is completely absorbed (ceases to exist).

mcqs.q: Compton scattering occurs when an x-ray photon:
opts: Interacts with an outer electron, ejecting it and being deflected (scattered)
Is completely absorbed by a K-shell electron
Is re-emitted with identical frequency and no electron loss
mcqs.explain: In Compton scattering the photon hits an outer-shell electron (recoil electron) and is deflected, continuing on to cause further ionisations.

mcqs.q: Coherent (Thomson) scattering involves a:
opts: Low-energy photon that is re-emitted scattered with the same frequency
High-energy photon ejecting a K-shell electron
mcqs.explain: In coherent (Thomson) scattering, a low-energy photon momentarily excites an outer electron, then the atom emits another photon of the same frequency in an altered (scattered) direction.

mcqs.q: The leaded-glass housing of the x-ray tube functions to:
opts: Prevent x-rays escaping in all directions except through the window
mcqs.explain: The leaded-glass vacuum housing stops x-rays escaping except through a central window, which lets the useful beam exit.

mcqs.q: Increasing the exposure time results in:
opts: A greater quantity (number) of x-ray photons
mcqs.explain: Exposure time controls quantity — a longer time means the filament emits electrons longer, producing more x-ray photons.

saqs.q: Who discovered x-rays and when, and what is ionizing radiation?
saqs.a: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, 1895 (Father of Radiology). Ionizing radiation = radiation able to produce ions by removing/adding an electron to an atom.

saqs.q: Describe the structure of the atom (Bohr model).
saqs.a: Nucleus with protons (+1) and neutrons (no charge); electrons (−) orbit in shells K,L,M,N,O,P,Q (2,8,18,32…). #electrons = #protons → neutral.

saqs.q: Name the parts of the cathode and the anode of the x-ray tube.
saqs.a: Cathode (−): tungsten filament + molybdenum focusing cup. Anode (+): tungsten target embedded in a copper block.

Bremsstrahlung: a high-speed electron is decelerated/deflected by the nucleus, emitting x-ray photons (most x-rays). Characteristic: an inner-shell electron is knocked out and replaced by an outer electron, releasing a characteristic photon.

saqs.q: List the factors controlling the x-ray beam and what each affects.
What do filtration and collimation achieve?
saqs.a: Filtration removes low-energy photons → reduces skin dose. Collimation controls beam size/shape → reduces tissue exposure.

saqs.q: Name and briefly describe the three interactions of x-rays with matter.
saqs.a: Coherent (Thomson): low-energy photon re-emitted scattered, same frequency. Photoelectric absorption: photon ejects a bound (K-shell) electron and is absorbed. Compton scattering: photon hits an outer electron and is deflected.
